Lieb-Schultz-Mattis in Higher Dimensions

M. B. Hastings Address:  Center for Nonlinear Studies and Theoretical Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM 87545, hastings@cnls.lanl.gov
July 28, 2003
Abstract

A generalization of the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem to higher dimensional spin systems is shown. The physical motivation for the result is that such spin systems typically either have long-range order, in which case there are gapless modes, or have only short-range correlations, in which case there are topological excitations. The result uses a set of loop operators, analogous to those used in gauge theories, defined in terms of the spin operators of the theory. We also obtain various cluster bounds on expectation values for gapped systems. These bounds are used, under the assumption of a gap, to rule out the first case of long-range order, after which we show the existence of a topological excitation. Compared to the ground state, the topologically excited state has, up to a small error, the same expectation values for all operators acting within any local region, but it has a different momentum.

]

I Introduction

Lieb, Schultz, and Mattis (LSM) proved in 1961 that a one-dimensional periodic chain of length LL, with half-integer spin per unit cell, has an excitation gap bounded by const./L{\rm const.}/L[1]. This behavior contrasts with the possibility of a Haldane gap in the integer spin case[2].

Despite several attempts[3, 4], this theorem has not been extended to higher dimensions. The basic difficulty in obtaining a higher-dimensional version of this theorem was pointed out in two insightful papers by Misguich and coworkers [5]: if spin correlations are short-ranged, the ground state wavefunction should be well described by a short-range resonating valence bond (RVB) state[6]. The short-range RVB basis decomposes into different topological sectors, depending upon the number of dimers crossing a given line through the system. This allows the construction of a low energy excited state very similar to the twisted state of LSM[7]. Instead, if spin correlations are long-ranged, such a state will not be low energy, but there will exist low energy spin wave excitations. In contrast to the one-dimensional case, there now exist two distinct means of obtaining a low energy excitation, significantly complicating the proof of any such theorem.

In the present paper, we show a higher-dimensional version of the LSM theorem. We consider a dd-dimensional system of spin-1/21/2 spins, with finite-range, S​U​(2)SU(2) invariant Hamiltonian ℋ\cal{H}, and with an odd number of spins per unit cell on the lattice. Define the total number of unit cells in the lattice to be VV. Let LL be the number of unit cells in one particular direction, and let LL be even; this direction will be referred to as the length. Therefore, VV is even (if VV were odd, there would be a trivial spin degeneracy). Let the system be periodic and translationally invariant in the length direction. Let V/LdV/L^{d} be bounded by a constant rr (this constant rr is arbitrary, and imposes some bound on the behavior of the aspect ratio of the system). Define V/LV/L to be the “width” of the system, and let this number be odd. Then, we show that if the ground state is unique, the gap Δ​E\Delta E to the first excited state satisfies,

Δ​E≤c​log⁡(L)/L,\Delta E\leq c\log(L)/L, (1)

where the constant cc depends on ℋ,d{\cal H},d, and where the result holds for all LL greater than some minimum L0L_{0}, where L0L_{0} depends on ℋ,d,r{\cal H},d,r[8].

In this paper, we use the term gap to deal specifically with the difference between the energy of the first excited state and the energy of the ground state. This includes two completely distinct physical cases. In the case of a one-dimensional system, a spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg chain has a continuous spectrum of excitations above the ground state. On the other hand, a Majumdar-Ghosh[9] chain has a doubly degenerate ground state with a gap to the next excited state. Weak perturbations of the Majumdar-Ghosh Hamiltonian can break the exact degeneracy between the two lowest states, leaving a system with a gap from the ground state to the first excited state which is exponentially small in the system size, and then a gap from the first excited state to the next excited state which is non-vanishing even in the limit of large system sizes. We consider both of these cases as systems in which the gap Δ​E\Delta E is vanishing in the limit of large system size. Although they are one-dimensional systems, these two cases closely match the two possibilities mentioned above for higher-dimensional systems. The first case involves a system with a continuous spectrum as it has algebraically decaying spin correlations. In the second case, the first excited state is very close to the twisted state of LSM.

The physical idea behind the proof of Eq. (1) is closely related to the two possibilities considered above for the absence of a gap. In the event of long-range order, or algebraic long-range order, one expects that there is no gap. Conversely, if there is a gap, one expects that there is no long-range order. This is the first statement we prove: we assume that the system has a gap Δ​E\Delta E and show, in section III, that connected expectation values decay exponentially in the spacing between them. Then, to prove Eq. (1) we first assume that Eq. (1) is violated, proceeding by contradiction. We assume the existence of such a gap violating Eq. (1) in sections IV, V, and VI. We then use the existence of the gap Δ​E\Delta E and the exponential decay of correlation functions to show an insensitivity of the system to boundary conditions in section IV. Then, this insensitivity is used to construct a low-energy, twisted state in section V. The construction of this twisted state will to some extent follow the topological attempt[4] at proving the LSM theorem in higher dimensions, with some important differences outlined below. In section VI we will show that the twisted state has a different momentum than the ground state. It is here that the odd width of the system becomes essential. Despite the different momentum compared to the ground state, the twisted state has, up to a small error, the same expectation values for all operators acting within any local region. Thus, we may refer to this state as a topologically excited state. Finally, in an appendix, we briefly consider a version of the result showing exponential decay of correlation functions for systems governed by certain Markov processes, rather than quantum systems.

Since we will constantly deal with operator equations of motion, we introduce a set of “loop operators” as a basic technique. The loop operators, which will be suitably defined products of spin operators, can be naturally interpreted as a product of gauge fields around a loop[10]. However, the use of these operators avoids the uncontrolled approximations associated with the U⁡(1)U(1) and Z2Z_{2} gauge theory techniques[11]. The introduction of these operators is not necessary to the main development, but provides a useful notation.

II Loop Algebra

We define operators iμ​ν≡12​δμ​ν+∑aSia​σaμ​νi^{\mu\nu}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\delta^{\mu\nu}+\sum_{a}S_{i}^{a}\sigma_{a}^{\mu\nu}, where SiaS_{i}^{a} are the spin operators at site ii and σa\sigma_{a} are the Pauli matrices, a=x,y,za=x,y,z. Thus, iμ​νi^{\mu\nu} is the two-by-two matrix of spin operators

(12+SizSix−i​SiySix+i​Siy12−Siz)\pmatrix{\frac{1}{2}+S^{z}_{i}&S^{x}_{i}-iS^{y}_{i}\cr S^{x}_{i}+iS^{y}_{i}&\frac{1}{2}-S^{z}_{i}\cr} (2)

We consider operators of the form iμ​ν​jν​ρ​kρ​σ​…​mα​μ,i^{\mu\nu}j^{\nu\rho}k^{\rho\sigma}...m^{\alpha\mu}, which we refer to as loop operators, where a summation over repeated indices is implied. Later we will often suppress the indices μ,ν\mu,\nu, writing ii rather than iμ​νi^{\mu\nu} to save space. Thus, we will write the loop operator mentioned above in the form tr⁡(i​j​k​…​m){\rm tr}(ijk...m), where the trace t​rtr refers to a trace over the Greek indices μ,ν,…\mu,\nu,.... Below we also use a trace T​rTr; this trace T​rTr refers to a trace of quantum operators, summing over all states in the Hilbert space of the system. Using the rule iμ​ν​iρ​σ=δν​ρ​iμ​σi^{\mu\nu}i^{\rho\sigma}=\delta^{\nu\rho}i^{\mu\sigma}, it is always possible to reduce a given product of traces to a new product such that each site appears only once. Then, an operator tr⁡(i​j​k​…​m){\rm tr}(ijk...m) permutes the spins around the sites i,j​…i,j...

Given an operator O⁡(t)O(t), the operator obeys the equation of motion ∂tO⁡(t)=−i⁡[O,ℋ]\partial_{t}O(t)=-i[O,{\cal H}]. Consider, for example a term tr⁡(i​j){\rm tr}(ij) in ℋ{\cal H}. We have [i,tr⁡(i​j)]=i​j−j​i[i,{\rm tr}(ij)]=ij-ji. As an illustration, let us give the full Greek indices on this commutator: we have [iμ​ν,(iα​β​jβ​α)]=iμ​α​jα​ν−jμ​α​iα​ν[i^{\mu\nu},(i^{\alpha\beta}j^{\beta\alpha})]=i^{\mu\alpha}j^{\alpha\nu}-j^{\mu\alpha}i^{\alpha\nu}, where summation over repeated indices α,β\alpha,\beta is assumed.

Introduce coordinates (x,y)(x,y) to specify sites ii, where xx labels the unit cells along the direction of length and is defined up to integer multiples of LL. The coordinate yy labels the unit cells along the other lattice directions, as well as labeling the particular spin within the unit cell. Given two sites ii and jj on the lattice, we define the distance between them, written |i−j||i-j|, as the minimum number of moves by lattice vectors needed to move from the unit cell containing ii to that containing jj. On a square lattice, for example, this is the Manhattan distance. Then, let RR denote the range of ℋ{\cal H}, the furthest distance between two sites in any term in ℋ{\cal H}. If all distances in a product of loops are less than L/2L/2, we can define a winding number of the given product around the lattice in the length direction. If all distances in the product remain less than L/2−RL/2-R, then the dynamics ∂tO=−i⁡[O,ℋ]{\partial_{t}O}=-i[O,{\cal H}] does not connect sectors with different winding numbers. We will make use of the coordinates later by sometimes writing loop operators tr⁡(i​j​…){\rm tr}(ij...) in the form tr⁡((x1,y1)​(x2,y2)​…){\rm tr}((x_{1},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})...), where ii has coordinates (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}), jj has coordinates (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}), and so on.

III Locality

We consider ground state expectation values of operators O1,O2​…O_{1},O_{2}..., written ⟨O1​(t1)​O2​(t2)​…⟩\langle O_{1}(t_{1})O_{2}(t_{2})...\rangle. The expectation values are not time ordered: the ordering of operators is as written. For a system with a unique ground state and an energy gap Δ​E\Delta E, on physical grounds one expects that connected correlation functions, defined as ⟨A⁡(0)​B​(0)⟩c≡⟨A⁡(0)​B​(0)⟩−⟨A⁡(0)⟩​⟨B⁡(0)⟩\langle A(0)B(0)\rangle_{c}\equiv\langle A(0)B(0)\rangle-\langle A(0)\rangle\langle B(0)\rangle, decay exponentially in distance (without loss of generality, we will assume ⟨A⟩=⟨B⟩=0\langle A\rangle=\langle B\rangle=0 through the rest of this section). The proof of this locality bound will be done in this section. We will do this in two steps: first, we consider commutators of the form [A⁡(t),B⁡(0)][A(t),B(0)], where A⁡(0)A(0) and B⁡(0)B(0) are separated in space. We bound the operator norm[13] of the commutator for sufficiently small tt, and thus bound its expectation value, in Eq. (4) below. The proof in this subsection will just be sketched; a more rigorous derivation is due to Lieb and Robinson[14]. This result provides a bound on the velocity of the system, as will be seen below. Then, in the next subsection, from this bound on the expectation value of the commutator and the existence of a gap, we use a spectral representation of the commutator to bound the connected correlation functions, thus obtaining the desired locality bound on the expectation value, Eq. (13). Finally, we close the section by giving a similar locality bound for operators separated in time.

III.2 Spectral Decomposition

Now, we use a spectral decomposition of f⁡(t)f(t) to relate f⁡(t)f(t) to the desired correlation function, ⟨A⁡(0)​B​(0)⟩\langle A(0)B(0)\rangle. Without loss of generality, let us set the ground state energy, E0E_{0}, to 00. The spectral decomposition of f⁡(t)f(t) gives

f⁡(t)=∑i(e−i​Ei​t​A0​i​Bi​0−ei​Ei​t​B0​i​Ai​0),f(t)=\sum_{i}(e^{-iE_{i}t}A_{0i}B_{i0}-e^{iE_{i}t}B_{0i}A_{i0}), (5)

where Ai​0A_{i0} is the matrix element of operator AA between the ground state 00 and the eigenstate ii, with energy Ei≥Δ​EE_{i}\geq\Delta E above the ground state energy, and similarly for the other A0​i,Bi​0,B0​iA_{0i},B_{i0},B_{0i}. There are no terms in Eq. (5) involving A00,B00A_{00},B_{00} since we have assumed ⟨A⟩=⟨B⟩=0\langle A\rangle=\langle B\rangle=0.

Let us define a function f+​(t)=∑ie−Ei​t​A0​i​Bi​0f^{+}(t)=\sum_{i}e^{-E_{i}t}A_{0i}B_{i0}, which thus contains only the negative frequency (positive energy) terms in f⁡(t)f(t). The significance of f+​(t)f^{+}(t) is that f+​(t)=⟨A⁡(t)​B​(0)⟩f^{+}(t)=\langle A(t)B(0)\rangle, so that the positive energy part of f⁡(t)f(t) contains the desired correlation function in it. IV Twisted Boundary Conditions

In this section we derive some results on the sensitivity to boundary conditions, as a step towards the the main result, Eq. (1). To derive a contradiction later, we will assume throughout this and the next two sections that there is a gap Δ​E\Delta E that violates Eq. (1), with an appropriately chosen cc. In the first subsection, we review the twist of boundary conditions and the topological attempt at proving the LSM theorem. In the second subsection, we show the specific results on the sensitivity to boundary conditions.

IV.1 Topological Argument

Here we will define a new twisted Hamiltonian, making use of the coordinates, (x,y)(x,y), introduced previously for lattice sites ii. To define the new twisted Hamiltonian, ℋθ,θ′{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}, replace all loop operators tr⁡((x1,y1)​(x2,y2)​(x3,y3)​…){\rm tr}((x_{1},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})(x_{3},y_{3})...) in ℋ{\cal H} with tr⁡((x1,y1)​R​(x1,x2)​(x2,y2)​R​(x2,x3)​(x3,y3)​…){\rm tr}((x_{1},y_{1})R(x_{1},x_{2})(x_{2},y_{2})R(x_{2},x_{3})(x_{3},y_{3})...). Here, the twist operator Rμ​ν​(x1,x2)≡exp⁡[±i​θ2​σzμ​ν]R^{\mu\nu}(x_{1},x_{2})\equiv\exp[\pm i\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_{z}^{\mu\nu}] if the shortest lattice path between x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} crosses from x=0x=0 to x=1x=1, where the sign is positive if the path crosses in the direction of increasing xx and negative if it crosses in the opposite direction. Here, Rμ​ν​(x1,x2)R^{\mu\nu}(x_{1},x_{2}) is a two-by-two matrix of numbers, rather than of operators,

Rμ​ν=(exp⁡[±i​θ2]00exp⁡[∓i​θ2])R^{\mu\nu}=\pmatrix{\exp[\pm i\frac{\theta}{2}]&0\cr 0&\exp[\mp i\frac{\theta}{2}]\cr} (17)

Alternately, if the shortest lattice path between x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} crosses from L/2L/2 to L/2+1L/2+1, Rμ​ν​(x1,x2)≡exp⁡[±i​θ′2​σzμ​ν]R^{\mu\nu}(x_{1},x_{2})\equiv\exp[\pm i\frac{\theta^{\prime}}{2}\sigma_{z}^{\mu\nu}]. Otherwise, R⁡(x1,x2)=δμ​νR(x_{1},x_{2})=\delta^{\mu\nu}. In Fig. (2), we show the coordinate system using x,yx,y and show where the two boundary condition twists are inserted.

Let us see what the effect of this twist is in terms of spin operators. Consider two sites, i,ji,j. Suppose the Hamiltonan ℋ0,0{\cal H}_{0,0} has a term such as tr⁡(i​j)=2​(Siz​Sjz+Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)+1/2{\rm tr}(ij)=2(S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}+S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j})+1/2. Then, let us suppose ii has x=0x=0 while jj has x=1x=1. Then, ℋθ,θ′{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}} has a term tr⁡(i​R​(0,1)​j​R​(1,0)){\rm tr}(iR(0,1)jR(1,0)). In terms of spin operators, this is equal to 2​[Siz​Sjz+cos⁡(θ)​(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)+sin⁡(θ)​(Six​Sjy−Siy​Sjx)]+1/22[S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}+\cos(\theta)(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j})+\sin(\theta)(S^{x}_{i}S^{y}_{j}-S^{y}_{i}S^{x}_{j})]+1/2. In the untwisted Hamiltonian, we coupled the dot product of the two spin vectors, S→i,S→j\vec{S}_{i},\vec{S}_{j}; in the twisted Hamiltonian, we couple them after rotating one by an angle θ\theta about the zz-axis. A good discussion of twists can be found in [5].

We have considered two different twist angles, θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime}. The spectrum of ℋθ,θ′{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}} depends only on the combination θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}. Further, from any given eigenfunction ψ⁡(θ,θ′)\psi(\theta,\theta^{\prime}) of ℋθ,θ′{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}, one can find an eigenfunction ψ⁡(θ−δ​θ,θ′+δ​θ)\psi(\theta-\delta\theta,\theta^{\prime}+\delta\theta) of ℋθ−δ​θ,θ′+δ​θ{\cal H}_{\theta-\delta\theta,\theta^{\prime}+\delta\theta} by ψ⁡(θ−δ​θ,θ′+δ​θ)=∏jei​δ​θ​Sjz​ψ​(θ,θ′)\psi(\theta-\delta\theta,\theta^{\prime}+\delta\theta)=\prod_{j}e^{i\delta\theta S^{z}_{j}}\psi(\theta,\theta^{\prime}), where the product extends over all sites j=(x,y)j=(x,y) with 0<x≤L/20<x\leq L/2.

Given that the spectrum depends only on the combination θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}, the reader may wonder what the reason is for introducing two twist angles, rather than just one angle. In fact, the second angle is a useful trick, introduced for the following reason: we have previously shown that the existence of a gap causes correlation functions to decay exponentially in the separation of the two operators. However, physically, one expects that the existence of a gap will also imply some insensitivity of the system to boundary conditions, enabling us to bound, for example, the second derivative of the ground state energy with respect to θ\theta. What we will do in the next subsection is show this insensitivity by using the fact that the spectrum depends only on θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime} to convert the second derivative (∂θ2\partial_{\theta}^{2}) of the ground state energy into a mixed partial derivative (∂θ∂θ′\partial_{\theta}\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}) of the ground state energy, and by then evaluating that mixed partial derivative as a correlation function, using the exponential decay of correlation functions. This will be stated more precisely at the start of the next subsection; we mention it here for motivation.

The eigenvalues are of ℋθ,θ′\cal{H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}} are invariant under θ+θ′→θ+θ′+2​π\theta+\theta^{\prime}\rightarrow\theta+\theta^{\prime}+2\pi, while the wavefunctions are invariant under θ+θ′→θ+θ′+4​π\theta+\theta^{\prime}\rightarrow\theta+\theta^{\prime}+4\pi[4, 5]. To motivate the results in this section, we recall the basic idea of the topological attempt[4] at proving the LSM. The idea is that if there is a gap at θ+θ′=0\theta+\theta^{\prime}=0, and if the gap remains open for all θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}, then under an adiabatic change in the angle θ\theta with θ′\theta^{\prime} fixed at zero, the ground state at θ=0\theta=0 evolves into the ground state at θ=2​π\theta=2\pi. At θ=2​π\theta=2\pi, the Hamiltonian is returned to the original Hamiltonian, but, for a system of odd width, the ground state expectation value of the translation operator changes sign, as will be discussed in more detail below. This leads to a contradiction: from the ground state with given expectation value of the translation operator, we construct another ground state with the opposite expectation value. The requirement that the topological attempt requires the gap to remain open for all θ\theta was pointed out in [5].

What the topological argument actually succeeds in showing is that the gap must close at some value of θ\theta. However, in order to use this argument to obtain any bound on the magnitude of the gap at θ=0\theta=0, we would have to show that a sufficiently large gap at θ=0\theta=0 would prevent the gap from closing for all θ\theta; that would then lead to a contradiction, enabling us to bound the gap at θ=0\theta=0. What we will see is that we can partially show this: for sufficiently large cc in Eq. (1), we can show to second order in θ\theta (or indeed, to any finite order) a bound on the change in ground state energy with respect to θ\theta. However, we will be unable to show that the gap remains open for all θ\theta because to bound the change in ground state energy for higher orders in θ\theta requires progressively increasing the constant cc in Eq. (1), and it is not possible to show the result to all orders. Thus, the topological attempt will ultimately fail, and we will give a physical example of how this can happen. In the next section (V), we will give a successful argument.

IV.2 Boundary Condition Sensitivity

We now show an insensitivity of the ground state energy, E0​(θ,θ′)E_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}), to second order[18] in the twist angle, θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}. At θ=θ′=0\theta=\theta^{\prime}=0, ∂θE0​(θ,θ′)=⟨∂θℋθ,θ′⟩=0\partial_{\theta}E_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})=\langle\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}\rangle=0. Indeed, taking any odd number of derivatives of E0​(θ,θ′)E_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}) leads to a vanishing quantity[19]. To second order in θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime}, we write a power series: E0​(θ,θ′)=E0​(0,0)+a​θ2/2+a​θ′2/2+b​θ​θ′E_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})=E_{0}(0,0)+a\theta^{2}/2+a\theta^{\prime 2}/2+b\theta\theta^{\prime}, where a=∂θ2E0=∂θ′2E0a=\partial_{\theta}^{2}E_{0}=\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}^{2}E_{0} and b=∂θ​θ′E0b=\partial_{\theta\theta^{\prime}}E_{0}. We will show that, for any given negative power of LL, we can find a constant cc such if Eq. (1) is violated for that cc, then aa is bounded by an ℋ{\cal H}-dependent constant times the given negative power of LL. We do this by calculating bb as a correlation function, and then showing that b=ab=a.

Recall linear perturbation theory: suppose a Hamiltonian ℋ{\cal H} is changed by some δ​ℋ\delta{\cal H}. For a non-degenerate state, |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, with eigenvalue EE, the change |δ​ψ⟩|\delta\psi\rangle in |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is given to linear order in δ​ℋ\delta{\cal H} by |δ​ψ⟩=(E−ℋ)−1​δ​ℋ​|ψ⟩|\delta\psi\rangle=(E-{\cal H})^{-1}\delta{\cal H}|\psi\rangle. Since the ground state is the lowest energy state, all other states have energies greater than it. Thus, we can write the change in the ground state to linear order as |δψ0⟩=−∑a≠0∫0∞dτe(E0−Ea)​τ|ψa⟩⟨ψa|δℋ|ψ0⟩=−∫0∞dτδℋ(iτ)|ψ0⟩|\delta\psi_{0}\rangle=-\sum_{a\neq 0}\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}\tau e^{(E_{0}-E_{a})\tau}|\psi_{a}\rangle\langle\psi_{a}|\delta{\cal H}|\psi_{0}\rangle=-\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}\tau\delta{\cal H}(i\tau)|\psi_{0}\rangle, where |ψ0⟩|\psi_{0}\rangle is the ground state wavefunction, |ψa⟩|\psi_{a}\rangle are a complete set of intermediate states, and where δ​ℋ​(i​τ)=exp⁡[−ℋ​τ]​δ​ℋ​exp⁡[ℋ​τ]\delta{\cal H}(i\tau)=\exp[-{\cal H}\tau]\delta{\cal H}\exp[{\cal H}\tau] is the change in the Hamiltonian operator, taken at imaginary time i​τi\tau. Here we have set E0​(0,0)=0E_{0}(0,0)=0 without loss of generality.

Specializing to the case of δ​ℋ=∂θℋθ,θ′\delta{\cal H}=\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}} and writing the change in ψ0\psi_{0} in terms of the θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime}-dependent ground state density matrix ρ0​(θ,θ′)≡|ψ0​(θ,θ′)⟩​⟨ψ0​(θ,θ′)|\rho^{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\equiv|\psi_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\rangle\langle\psi_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})| we have:

∂θ′ρ0=−∫0∞dτ∂θ′ℋθ,θ′(iτ)ρ0−∫−∞0dτρ0∂θ′ℋθ,θ′(iτ).\displaystyle\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}\rho^{0}=-\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}\tau\,\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}(i\tau)\rho^{0}-\int_{-\infty}^{0}{\rm d}\tau\,\rho^{0}\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}(i\tau).

Note that since ⟨δ​ℋ⟩\langle\delta{\cal H}\rangle vanishes in this case, we do not need to worry about matrix elements of δ​ℋ\delta{\cal H} from the ground state to the ground state.

Now, we can use the change in the density matrix to compute bb by b=Tr⁡[(∂θ′ℋθ,θ′)​(∂θρ0)]b={\rm Tr}[(\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}})(\partial_{\theta}\rho^{0})]. So,

OPEN−⟨∂θ′ℋθ,θ′​(−i​τ)​∂θℋθ,θ′​(0)⟩),\displaystyle-\langle\partial_{\theta^{\prime}}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}(-i\tau)\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}(0)\rangle\Bigr),

where the derivatives are evaluated at θ=θ′=0\theta=\theta^{\prime}=0. The derivative ∂θℋi\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{i} is non-vanishing only for sites ii which are within distance RR of x=0x=0; there are at most S​V/LSV/L such sites. For each ii, ‖∂θℋi‖≤J​S||\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{i}||\leq JS, so ‖∂θℋθ,θ′‖≤J​S2​V/L||\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}||\leq JS^{2}V/L. Second, we can use Eq. (16) to bound each correlation function by

Also, we have used l=L/2l=L/2, ignoring the slight error, that in fact l≥L/2−Rl\geq L/2-R. Finally, we have used NB≤SN_{B}\leq S in Eq. (20).

where x=2S(1+1/π​c1​L​Δ​E)exp[−c1ΔE(L/2)/2]x=2S(1+1/\sqrt{\pi c_{1}L\Delta E})\exp[-c_{1}\Delta E(L/2)/2]. Thus, |b|≤2​(J​S2​V/L)2​(x/Δ​E)​(1+log⁡(x))|b|\leq 2(JS^{2}V/L)^{2}(x/\Delta E)(1+\log(x)). The number of sites, VV, is bounded by r​LdrL^{d}, while for Δ​E\Delta E greater than c​ln​(L)/Lc{\rm ln}(L)/L, xx is bounded by a cc-dependent negative power of LL. Therefore, we can bound |b||b| by any desired negative power of LL by choosing cc sufficiently large.

However, E0​(θ,−θ)=E0​(0,0)E_{0}(\theta,-\theta)=E_{0}(0,0), so b=ab=a. Thus, we have also bounded |a||a| by the same negative power of LL. Therefore, at θ=θ′=0\theta=\theta^{\prime}=0, we find that |∂θ2E0​(θ,θ′)||\partial_{\theta}^{2}E_{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})| is bounded by a negative power of LL. This shows some insensitivity of the ground state energy to boundary conditions. This realizes the physical idea[5] that a spin liquid state is defined by the lack of response to a twist in boundary conditions to second order in θ\theta[20].

At fourth order in θ\theta, we must evaluate a correlation function of four operators, each of order J​S2​V/LJS^{2}V/L; to bound these correlation functions requires a larger cc. Each higher order in θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime} requires an even larger cc, so that it is not possible to bound the change in ground state energy for arbitrary θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}. Therefore, the topological attempt[4] to establish the LSM result fails. Indeed, a gap at θ+θ′=0\theta+\theta^{\prime}=0 must close for θ+θ′≠0\theta+\theta^{\prime}\neq 0[5].

It is worth giving a specific physical example of this possibility, as the topological argument does show that the gap must close for some θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}. In many physical examples of spin liquids, the closing of the gap arises because a state which is at some very low energy, of order J​L−1JL^{-1} or less, above the ground state at θ+θ′=0\theta+\theta^{\prime}=0 crosses the ground state energy at a finite θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}. For example, if the Majumdar-Ghosh Hamiltonian is slightly perturbed, there is a state at an exponentially small energy above the ground state which crosses the ground state at θ+θ′=π\theta+\theta^{\prime}=\pi.

However, it is also possible for a state which is at some energy J​L0JL^{0} to cross the ground state: consider a system with two competing phases, one of which is a spin liquid phase while the other is a spin ordered phase with a spiral order. The spiral order is chosen so that the spin ordered phase can be frustrated at θ+θ′=0\theta+\theta^{\prime}=0, and the spin liquid is the ground state there. At some θ+θ′≠0\theta+\theta^{\prime}\neq 0, however, the spiral phase can take over as the ground state. This taking over as the ground state can happen either via a level crossing (if the two states have different symmetry, for example, or if the spin ordered phase has a non-vanishing net spin), or via an avoided crossing. This provides a specific example of a system in which a state or phase which is at an energy of order J​L0JL^{0} at θ+θ′=0\theta+\theta^{\prime}=0 becomes the ground state at some non-vanishing θ+θ′\theta+\theta^{\prime}.

The solution to this problem is simple: it is not necessary to show that there is a gap for all twist angles. Instead, we start with the ground state at vanishing twist and continuously evolve this state, obtaining a state for any twist angle which is an approximate eigenstate of the twisted Hamiltonian, not necessarily the ground state. This approximate eigenstate will be explicitly constructed in the next section, while in the section after that we demonstrate that at a twist of 2​π2\pi the expectation value of the translation operator has changed sign in the new state compared to the ground state. Thus, this gives a new low energy state, different from the ground state.

V Twisting the Ground State

V.1 Constructing the Twisted State

Let ρ⁡(θ,0)\rho(\theta,0) be a θ\theta-dependent density matrix that we construct below. Divide the system into two overlapping halves: half (1) contains sites with x=3​L/4−R,3​L/4−R+1,…,L−1,0,1,…​L/4+Rx=3L/4-R,3L/4-R+1,...,L-1,0,1,...L/4+R, while half (2) contains sites with x=L/4−R,L/4−R+1,…,3​L/4+Rx=L/4-R,L/4-R+1,...,3L/4+R. That is, half (1) contains all sites from x=3​L/4−Rx=3L/4-R up to x=L−1x=L-1, as well as all sites from x=0x=0 up to L/4+RL/4+R, while half (2) contains all sites from x=L/4−Rx=L/4-R up to x=3​L/4+Rx=3L/4+R. The halves are shown as shaded regions in Fig. (3).

The reason we choose two overlapping halves is that we will be considering density matrices which involve only sites within a given half. These matrices will be defined by tracing over sites outside the given half. Then, to evaluate the expectation value of the energy of the system, we will be able to evaluate the expectation value as a sum of operators which lie completely within one or the other half. That is, by making the two halves overlap, we will deal with the question of the “seam” where the two halves join. This is mentioned here as motivation and will be done in more detail below.

Define ρ1​(θ,0)=Tr2​[ρ⁡(θ,0)]\rho_{1}(\theta,0)={\rm Tr}_{2}[\rho(\theta,0)], where Tr2{\rm Tr}_{2} denotes a trace over all sites not in half (1), and define ρ2​(θ,0)=Tr1​[ρ⁡(θ,0)]\rho_{2}(\theta,0)={\rm Tr}_{1}[\rho(\theta,0)], the trace over sites not in half (2). Similarly, define ρ10​(θ,θ′)=Tr2​[ρ0​(θ,θ′)]\rho_{1}^{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})={\rm Tr}_{2}[\rho^{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})], and ρ20​(θ,θ′)=Tr1​[ρ0​(θ,θ′)]\rho_{2}^{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})={\rm Tr}_{1}[\rho^{0}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})]. We will assume throughout this section that there is a gap violating Eq. (1). Then, for sufficiently large cc, we will construct ρ1\rho_{1} such that

ρ1​(θ,0)−E1​(θ)=(∏jei​θ​Sjz)​ρ10​(0,0)​(∏je−i​θ​Sjz)\displaystyle\rho_{1}(\theta,0)-E_{1}(\theta)=\Bigl(\prod_{j}e^{i\theta S^{z}_{j}}\Bigr)\rho_{1}^{0}(0,0)\Bigl(\prod_{j}e^{-i\theta S^{z}_{j}}\Bigr) (22)
=ρ10​(θ,−θ),\displaystyle=\rho_{1}^{0}(\theta,-\theta),

where the products extend over all sites j=(x,y)j=(x,y) with 0<x≤L/40<x\leq L/4 and where E1​(θ)E_{1}(\theta) is an error term such that the trace norm[21] |E1​(θ)||E_{1}(\theta)| is bounded by a constant times a negative power of LL for all 0≤θ≤2​π0\leq\theta\leq 2\pi. The particular negative power of LL can be determined by choosing the constant cc in Eq. (1). As a useful terminology, we will refer to a quantity as “small” if, for any desired negative power of LL, we can find sufficiently large cc or sufficiently large qq (introduced below), such that the given quantity is bounded by a constant times the given negative power of LL for all LL. Thus, we wish |E1​(θ)||E_{1}(\theta)| to be small. Note that, given this definition of small, if a small quantity is multiplied by any fixed power of LL, the result is a small quantity. Sometimes, we will indicate that a quantity is made small by choosing cc or by choosing qq, to specify which of the two needs to be made sufficiently large.

In differential form, we require

∂θρ1​(θ,0)=∑ji⁡[Sjz,ρ10​(θ,−θ)]+e1​(θ),\partial_{\theta}\rho_{1}(\theta,0)=\sum_{j}i[S^{z}_{j},\rho_{1}^{0}(\theta,-\theta)]+e_{1}(\theta), (23)

where e1=∂θE1e_{1}=\partial_{\theta}E_{1}. We will show that the upper[22] derivative 𝒟θ​|E1​(θ)|{\cal D}_{\theta}|E_{1}(\theta)| is small, from which Eq. (22) will follow. We will also require ρ2​(θ,0)=ρ20​(0,0)\rho_{2}(\theta,0)=\rho_{2}^{0}(0,0), up to a similarly bounded error term E2​(θ)E_{2}(\theta), and ∂θρ1​(θ,0)=e2​(θ)\partial_{\theta}\rho_{1}(\theta,0)=e_{2}(\theta), with a similarly bounded 𝒟θ​|E2​(θ)|{\cal D}_{\theta}|E_{2}(\theta)|.

The physical motivation behind Eq. (22) is to construct a state for the Hamiltonian ℋθ,0{\cal H}_{\theta,0} that has an energy close to E0​(0,0)E_{0}(0,0). The twist θ\theta is along a line that lies completely within half (1) while θ′\theta^{\prime} is along a line that lies completely within half (2). Within half (1), the Hamiltonians ℋθ,0{\cal H}_{\theta,0} and ℋθ,−θ{\cal H}_{\theta,-\theta} are equal, so we construct a density matrix such that within half (1) the given density matrix is close to the ground state density matrix of ℋθ,−θ{\cal H}_{\theta,-\theta}. Then, the expectation of any operator OO which lies completely within half (1) for the density matrix ρ⁡(θ,0)\rho(\theta,0) will be within ‖O‖​|E1​(θ)|||O|||E_{1}(\theta)| of the expectation value of that operator for the density matrix ρ⁡(θ,−θ)\rho(\theta,-\theta). On the other hand, within half (2), the Hamiltonians ℋθ,0{\cal H}_{\theta,0} and ℋ0,0{\cal H}_{0,0} are equal, so we also require that within half (2) the density matrix be close to the ground state density matrix of ℋ0,0{\cal H}_{0,0}.

Then, the expectation value of the energy in the state defined by ρ⁡(θ,0)\rho(\theta,0) is equal to Tr⁡[ρ⁡(θ,0)​ℋθ,0]{\rm Tr}[\rho(\theta,0){\cal H}_{\theta,0}]. Once we have shown that both Eq. (22) and the bound on |E2​(θ)||E_{2}(\theta)| are satisfied, it will follow that this expectation value will be within an amount ‖ℋθ,0‖​max​(|E1|,|E2|)||{\cal H}_{\theta,0}||{\rm max}(|E_{1}|,|E_{2}|) of E0​(0,0)E_{0}(0,0), since the Hamiltonian ℋ{\cal H} can be written as a sum of operators which are entirely within half (1) or entirely within half (2) (it was for this reason that the halves were chosen to overlap). Therefore, since ‖ℋ‖||{\cal H}|| is bounded by V​J<r​Ld​JVJ<rL^{d}J, if we pick cc in Eq. (1) sufficiently large, we will find that Tr⁡[ρ⁡(θ,0)​ℋθ,0]−E0​(0,0){\rm Tr}[\rho(\theta,0){\cal H}_{\theta,0}]-E_{0}(0,0) will also be small at θ=2​π\theta=2\pi; this follows from the statement that a small quantity multiplied by a fixed power of LL is also small.

Our claim, which we show in this section, is that Eq. (22) is satisfied by a ρ⁡(θ,0)\rho(\theta,0) defined as follows for 0≤θ≤2​π0\leq\theta\leq 2\pi. We pick

∂θρ(θ,0)=−∫0c1​Ldτ[A+(iτ)−A−(−iτ),ρ(θ,0)],\partial_{\theta}\rho(\theta,0)=-\int\limits_{0}^{c_{1}L}{\rm d}\tau\,[A^{+}(i\tau)-A^{-}(-i\tau),\rho(\theta,0)], (24)

where we define

A+(iτ)=(2π)−1exp[−(τΔE)2/(2qlog(L))]×\displaystyle A^{+}(i\tau)=(2\pi)^{-1}\exp[-(\tau\Delta E)^{2}/(2q\log(L))]\times (25)

Let the states have energy difference −ω=Ea−Eb-\omega=E_{a}-E_{b}. Then, doing the integral over tt we find that A+​(i​τ)A^{+}(i\tau) has a matrix element between states a,ba,b equal to exp⁡[ω​τ]​(∂θℋ)a​b\exp[\omega\tau](\partial_{\theta}{\cal H})_{ab} for −ω>0-\omega>0 and equal to zero for −ω<0-\omega<0. Similarly, A−​(−i​τ)A^{-}(-i\tau) has a matrix element equal to exp⁡[−ω​τ]​(∂θℋ)a​b\exp[-\omega\tau](\partial_{\theta}{\cal H})_{ab} for −ω<0-\omega<0 and equal to zero for −ω>0-\omega>0. Then, for any given time τ\tau, the integrand of Eq. (24) would be the same as that of Eq. (18) for θ=0\theta=0, since in that case the only non-vanishing terms in Eq. (24) are −A+​(i​τ)​ρ​(0,0)−ρ⁡(0,0)​A−​(−i​τ)-A^{+}(i\tau)\rho(0,0)-\rho(0,0)A^{-}(-i\tau).

What we will do later is to take a finite qq instead. Physically, this means that rather than taking an adiabatic change in θ\theta which keeps us in the ground state, we instead “pass through” the level crossing when the gap closes at some θ≠0\theta\neq 0, going from the ground state to some low energy excited state.

Eq. (24) gives the change in ρ\rho equal to the commutator of ρ\rho with an anti-Hermitian operator, and hence generates an infinitesimal unitary transformation of ρ\rho. Thus, ρ\rho continues to be a density matrix which projects onto a single state, defined to be ψ⁡(θ,0)\psi(\theta,0).

V.2 Bound on Error Terms

We now show that we can find a cc such that the definition (24) satisfies Eq. (23) in general. [A+(iτ)−A−(−iτ),ρ0(θ,−θ)]].\displaystyle[A^{+}(i\tau)-A^{-}(-i\tau),\rho^{0}(\theta,-\theta)]].

First, consider Eq. (28). In the definition of A+,−A^{+,-} as an integral over tt, the integral over times |t|>c1​(L/2−R)|t|>c_{1}(L/2-R) has an operator norm bounded by ||∂θℋ||∫|t|>c1​(L/2−R)exp[−(tΔE)2/(2qlog(L)]||\partial_{\theta}{\cal H}||\int_{|t|>c_{1}(L/2-R)}\exp[-(t\Delta E)^{2}/(2q\log(L)]. VI Translation Operator

Consider the operator tr⁡((1,y)​(2,y)​…​(L,y)){\rm tr}((1,y)(2,y)...(L,y)), which translates the sites with given yy. The translation operator TT which translates the entire system by one unit cell is the product of these loop operators over all yy (there are an odd number of such loop operators). The ground state of ℋ0,0{\cal H}_{0,0} is an eigenstate of TT. If the ground state is non-degenerate, then it has eigenvalue ±1\pm 1; without loss of generality we will assume in this section that is has eigenvalue +1+1.

In this section we will show that the expectation value of TT for ρ⁡(2​π,0)\rho(2\pi,0) is opposite to that for ρ⁡(0,0)\rho(0,0), up to small error. We note that if ℋθ,0{\cal H}_{\theta,0} were to have a gap for all 0≤θ≤2​π0\leq\theta\leq 2\pi, then the results in this section would provide the last step in the topological argument discussed above. Instead, the results in this section will complete the argument started in the previous section: ρ⁡(2​π,0)\rho(2\pi,0) gives us a density matrix such that Tr⁡[ρ⁡(2​π,0)​ℋθ,0]−E0​(0,0){\rm Tr}[\rho(2\pi,0){\cal H}_{\theta,0}]-E_{0}(0,0) is small, but which, up to small error, has the opposite expectation value for TT. Since the difference in the expectation of ℋ{\cal H} is small, we can find a cc such that the difference in expectation value decays faster than 1/L1/L, and then we can find an L0L_{0} such that for L>L0L>L_{0} the state ψ⁡(2​π,0)\psi(2\pi,0) has an energy expectation value which is less than c​ln​(L)/Lc{\rm ln}(L)/L above the ground state. However, since the expectation value of TT is opposite for ρ⁡(2​π,0)\rho(2\pi,0) compared to ρ⁡(0,0)\rho(0,0), up to small error, this state has an overlap on the ground state which is small. Thus, we will show in this section a contradiction under the assumption that the system had a gap Δ​E\Delta E which violated Eq. (1) and under the assumption that the system was translation symmetric, so that the ground state was an eigenstate of TT.

We first define a twisted translation operator, Tθ,θ′≡∏ytr⁡(exp⁡[i​θ2​σz]​(1,y)​(2,y)​…​(L/2,y)​exp​[i​θ′2​σz]​(L/2+1,y)​…​(L,y))T_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}\equiv\prod_{y}{\rm tr}(\exp[i\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_{z}](1,y)(2,y)...(L/2,y)\exp[i\frac{\theta^{\prime}}{2}\sigma_{z}](L/2+1,y)...(L,y)). Then, Tθ,θ′T_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}} is a unitary operator and a symmetry of ℋθ,θ′{\cal H}_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}}. Finally, given that T​ψ0​(0,0)=ψ0​(0,0)T\psi_{0}(0,0)=\psi_{0}(0,0), we have Tθ,−θ​ψ0​(θ,−θ)=ψ0​(θ,−θ)T_{\theta,-\theta}\psi_{0}(\theta,-\theta)=\psi_{0}(\theta,-\theta) for all θ\theta.

VII Discussion

The main result is Eq. (1), obtaining a bound on the energy gap for spin models in arbitrary dimensions. In order to obtain this result, we have introduced a set of loop operators, and proven a bound on connected correlation functions. This bound on correlation functions did not rely on the system being a spin system; rather, it is valid for any Hamiltonian such that the ℋi{\cal H}_{i} have bounded operator norm, and such that the interaction is finite range. Below, we generalize this bound on correlation functions to certain other systems as well.

We note that for the case of higher spin representations of S​U​(2)SU(2), Eq. (1) follows automatically from the result for spin-1/21/2, so long as the total spin within all unit cells is half-odd: the higher spins can be written as various combinations of spin-1/21/2 spins, and if the total spin in the unit cell is half-odd then there will result an odd number of spin-1/21/2 spins in each unit cell. Suppose, for example, a unit cell contains one spin-11 spin and one spin-1/21/2 spin, giving a total spin of 3/23/2 which is half-odd. Then, the spin-1 can be written as two spin-1/21/2 spins. Let these two spins be called S1,S2S_{1},S_{2} and let the Hamiltonian include only terms symmetric under interchange of S1,S2S_{1},S_{2}. This new Hamiltonian has three spin-1/21/2 spins in each unit cell, and hence falls within the class of Hamiltonians considered above. Then, there are two different sectors of the Hilbert space with no terms in the Hamiltonian coupling these two sectors: one sector in which S1,S2S_{1},S_{2} form a spin-00, and one in which they form a spin-11. By adding a term coupling S1S_{1} to S2S_{2} to the Hamiltonian with a sufficiently large, negative (ferromagnetic) coefficient, we can ensure that the ground and first excited states lie in the sector in which S1,S2S_{1},S_{2} have total spin-11. Then, the existence of a low-lying state satisfying Eq. (1) for the new system with only spin-1/21/2 implies the existence of such a low-lying state for the original system with both spin-11 and spin-1/21/2. It would also be interesting to generalize these results to other groups S​U​(N)SU(N), as well as to consider the case of even V/LV/L.

We finish with two conjectures. First, we conjecture that the same Eq. (1) holds for systems with an even width, so long as the width V/LV/L is of order Ld−1L^{d-1} and so long as d>1d>1. For d=1d=1, this result is of course not true, as Haldane gap behavior is possible.

Second, consider the thermal expectation value of TT at an inverse temperature β\beta, defined by ⟨T⟩β≡Tr⁡[exp⁡(−β​ℋ)​T]/Tr⁡[exp⁡(−β​ℋ)]\langle T\rangle_{\beta}\equiv{\rm Tr}[\exp(-\beta{\cal H})T]/{\rm Tr}[\exp(-\beta{\cal H})]. We conjecture that there is a constant cc, depending on ℋ,d{\cal H},d such that for β>c​log⁡(L)/L\beta>c\log(L)/L the given thermal expectation value ⟨T⟩β\langle T\rangle_{\beta} vanishes in the limit L→∞L\rightarrow\infty for systems of odd width. We base this conjecture on the following physical observations: for ferromagnetic systems, there are spin wave excitations, with dispersion relation E∝k2E\propto k^{2}. It may be shown that the presence of these excitations causes ⟨T⟩β\langle T\rangle_{\beta} to vanish for β\beta of order LL as L→∞L\rightarrow\infty. For antiferromagnetic systems, the translation symmetry is broken by the antiferromagnetic ordering (in fact, for these systems, the true ground state has translation symmetry and is a superposition of different broken symmetry states, but there are low-lying states with different expectation values of TT so that for β\beta of order LL, the expectation value ⟨T⟩β\langle T\rangle_{\beta} vanishes). Finally, for spin liquid systems, there is a low-lying excited state with the opposite expectation value of TT compared to the ground state, as we have found above. We leave a proof of both of these conjectures for future work.

Appendix A Markov Processes and Locality

Consider a system with a probability pip_{i} of being in state ii and a transition matrix Ti​jT_{ij} so that the equation of motion is ∂tpi=∑jTi​j​pj\partial_{t}p_{i}=\sum_{j}T_{ij}p_{j}. For the total probability to be conserved, we have ∑iTi​j=0\sum_{i}T_{ij}=0, which guarantees that Ti​jT_{ij} has at least one zero eigenvalue. Let us assume, further, that all eigenvalues of Ti​jT_{ij} are real. This includes all systems for which the stationary state (given by the zero eigenvector of Ti​jT_{ij}) obeys detailed balance. A typical example of such a process would be the Monte Carlo dynamics of a statistical mechanics system. We will first derive a suitable generalization of the locality result (13) to systems governed by such a Markov process, and then discuss the implication for statistical mechanics systems.

Let us assume that the spectrum of TT is such that there is only one zero eigenvalue, with right eigenvector pi0p_{i}^{0}, and that all other eigenvalues λ\lambda are negative with λ≤−Δ\lambda\leq-\Delta, for some Δ>0\Delta>0. Assume pi0p_{i}^{0} is normalized by ∑ipi0=1\sum_{i}p_{i}^{0}=1.

Then, introduce various quantities to be measured, A,B,…A,B,..., so that the expectation value of AA is given by ⟨A⟩=∑iAi​pi0\langle A\rangle=\sum_{i}A_{i}p_{i}^{0}. We can write this slightly differently by introducing for each such quantity a diagonal matrix given by A^i​i=Ai\hat{A}_{ii}=A_{i} for all ii and A^i​j=0\hat{A}_{ij}=0 for i≠ji\neq j. Further, introduce an additional vector IiI_{i}, such that Ii=1I_{i}=1 for all ii. This vector IiI_{i} is a left eigenvector of TT with zero eigenvalue, since ∑iTi​j=0\sum_{i}T_{ij}=0 as mentioned above. Then, ⟨A⟩=Ii​Ai​j​pj0\langle A\rangle=I_{i}A_{ij}p_{j}^{0}.

We can now consider expectation values of quantities at different times: ⟨A⁡(t)​B​(0)⟩≡I†​A^​exp​[T​t]​B^​p0=I†​exp​[−T​t]​A^​exp​[T​t]​B^​p0=I†​A^​(t)​B^​(0)​p0\langle A(t)B(0)\rangle\equiv I^{\dagger}\hat{A}\exp[Tt]\hat{B}p^{0}=I^{\dagger}\exp[-Tt]\hat{A}\exp[Tt]\hat{B}p^{0}=I^{\dagger}\hat{A}(t)\hat{B}(0)p^{0}. In these equations, I†I^{\dagger} denotes the transpose of the vector II (II is real, so no complex conjugation is necessary), and we have left off all the indices on vectors I,pI,p and matrices A,B,exp⁡[±T​t]A,B,\exp[\pm Tt]: the product is evaluated following the usual rules of matrix multiplication. In the sequence of equalities above, the first equality defines the time evolution of the system, the second equality follows since I​exp⁡[−T​t]=II\exp[-Tt]=I, and the last equality follows since we define A^​(t)\hat{A}(t) by the equation of motion: ∂tA^​(t)=[A⁡(t),T]\partial_{t}\hat{A}(t)=[A(t),T]. It is then possible to extend this definition to operators separated by an imaginary time separation: ⟨A⁡(i​t)​B​(0)⟩\langle A(it)B(0)\rangle.

Now, consider a typical physical example: an Ising system, governed by Monte Carlo spin flip dynamics, with A⁡(0),B⁡(0)A(0),B(0) representing the value of two different spins which are separated in space. In such a case (as well as in many others), it is possible to obtain a bound similar to Eq. (4). Assume that the matrix TT can be written as a sum of matrices TiT_{i}, with finite interaction range RR and with a bound ‖Ti‖≤J||{T}_{i}||\leq J, where ii is a site index. Define f⁡(t)≡⟨[A⁡(i​t),B⁡(0)]⟩f(t)\equiv\langle[A(it),B(0)]\rangle. Since f⁡(t)≤‖[A⁡(i​t),B⁡(0)]‖f(t)\leq||[A(it),B(0)]||,

f⁡(t)≤2​NB​S​‖A‖​‖B‖​|2​J​S​t|l/2​R​e2​J​S​|t|(l/2​R)!\displaystyle f(t)\leq\frac{2N_{B}S||A||||B|||2JSt|^{l/2R}e^{2JS|t|}}{(l/2R)!} (36)
≡NB​‖A‖​‖B‖​g​(t,l).\displaystyle\equiv N_{B}||A||||B||g(t,l).

At this point, from the existence of a Δ>0\Delta>0 and a spectral representation with all eigenvalues real[24] follows a result similar to Eq. (13):

|⟨A⁡(0)​B​(0)⟩c|≤12​π​2​NB​‖A‖||B||g⁡(c1​l,l)+\displaystyle|\langle A(0)B(0)\rangle_{c}|\leq\frac{1}{2\pi}2N_{B}||A||||B||g(c_{1}l,l)+ (37)
2(1+12​π​c1​l​Δ​E)||A||||B||e−c1ΔEl/2.\displaystyle 2(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi c_{1}l\Delta E}})||A||||B||e^{-c_{1}\Delta El/2}.

Therefore, if there is a Markov dynamics that gives rise to the equilibrium probability distribution pi0p_{i}^{0} which has a Δ>0\Delta>0, then there is an exponential decay of correlation functions in space. An example is a spin system in the paramagnetic phase with Monte Carlo spin flip dynamics. The converse is not necessarily true: a spin system in the paramagnetic phase with spin exchange dynamics does not have a Δ>0\Delta>0 but instead has spin correlations which decay with a power law time. However, this dynamics gives rise to the same equilibrium probability distribution as the spin flip dynamics does, and hence has exponentially decaying correlations in space.
